Use provocative testing with the insulin tolerance test (ITT) or growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH)-arginine to establish the diagnosis of GHD. C
Start treatment with low doses of recombinant growth hormone (GH) and titrate every 1 to 2 months based on clinical, biochemical (insulin-like growth factor-I [IGF-I]), and/or adverse responses. B
Children diagnosed and treated at an early age with appropriate dosing of recombinant GH can achieve adult stature in the normal adult range. B

background.definition: GHD is a clinical syndrome caused by absolute or relative deficiency of GH, a neuroendocrine hormone responsible for longitudinal growth of bone and muscle (ie, height) in children and many metabolic functions in adults. The specific symptoms are highly variable and depend on the age of onset and severity of the deficiency.

list.listitem: In a study of 80,000 Utah children in 1994, the prevalence of GHD was 1 per 3480.
As many as 70% of patients with childhood GHD will have persistence of GHD into adulthood.

The only study to measure incidence and prevalence directly in adults was done in Denmark and found an annual incidence rate of 1.4 per 100,000 in females and 1.9 per 100,000 in males. The prevalence was 1 in 2480.
In 1999, about 18,500 children received GH to treat idiopathic or organic GHD.

Many cases of GHD are genetic, although multiple mutations and patterns of inheritance are demonstrated. The genetic basis accounts for most cases in children, although children can acquire GHD through the same secondary causes that occur in adults.
In adults, more than 90% of patients develop GHD due to pituitary disorders such as pituitary tumors, surgery, or radiation therapy for the tumor.
Traumatic brain injury (GHD occurs in 27% of patients) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (GHD occurs in 47% of patients) are increasingly important causes.
GH is synthesized, stored, and secreted by the anterior pituitary. Secretion is regulated by hypothalamic hormones including (stimulates) and somatostatin (inhibits).
GH is released in a pulsatile fashion following a circadian rhythm. Secretion increases markedly during puberty but returns to baseline levels in adulthood.

Exercise, stress, slow wave sleep, fasting/starvation, and drops in serum glucose levels stimulate GH secretion. Rapid eye movement sleep, aging, obesity, both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, and postprandial hyperglycemia inhibit GH secretion. A wide variety of other hormones stimulate and inhibit secretion as well.
The primary effect of GH is stimulating the secretion of IGF-I, which has wide effects on many metabolic functions.
There is no role for routine screening of asymptomatic adults. C

Currently there are no recommendations for routine screening of children. A meta-analysis from Great Britain showed that programs screening simple height measurements at school entry detect 1 case of GHD for every 4,000 to 20,000 children screened. These programs cost between $40,000 and $60,000 per quality-adjusted life year saved, but most of these costs came from further evaluation and treatment, so the incremental costs may have actually been less. B

If height is used as a screening measure, plot the child's height on age, gender, race, and environmentally appropriate growth charts. Evaluate a child who falls below the 5 percentile for GHD. If only a single data point is available, it may be reasonable to wait 6 to 12 months to assess growth velocity, unless the child is nearing puberty. A growth velocity below the 10 percentile should prompt further evaluation. B
Consider GHD in adults who have a history of hypothalamic/pituitary disease, intracranial surgery, or irradiation, and in children who are more than 2 SDs below average height for age. B
Use provocative testing with the ITT or GHRH-arginine to establish the diagnosis of GHD. C
The GHRH-arginine test may be less accurate in patients with acute GHD of a hypothalamic origin (ie, recent irradiation). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Abnormal upper segment: lower segment ratio (should be 1:1 in adults)
Sudden change in growth velocity (as opposed to constant low growth velocity)
Presence of other endocrine anomalies (thyroid is most common)
Identified by careful history and examination

list.listitem: Adults: GHD can cause a variety of symptoms related to decreased metabolic function and disturbances in insulin/glucose metabolism. Nonspecific but common signs and symptoms include fatigue, decreased strength, poor exercise tolerance, weight loss or weight gain, decreased muscle mass, visceral obesity, emotional lability, anxiety, decreased libido, and sleep difficulties.

None of these findings are pathognomonic for adult GHD, and some patients with GHD may be asymptomatic. Consider GHD in adults with any of the symptoms or signs mentioned above, especially with a history of intracranial surgery, radiation exposure, traumatic brain injury, or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Children: GHD in children generally presents with constant low growth velocity producing height that is more than 2 SDs below the mean for age (and is often >3 SDs below the mean or <0.4 percentile). Height velocity is often less than the 10 percentile for age. GHD also affects multiple aspects of skeletal and hormonal maturation. Children with GHD may have immature facies, truncal obesity, delayed dentition, and late onset of puberty; male children may have a small phallus.

Serum GH levels vary widely throughout the day. Single, random measures of GH are meaningless in the evaluation of suspected GHD. Tests designed to measure the secretion of GH in response to a measured stimulus (provocative tests) are required for accurate diagnosis.

The ITT is the gold standard. This test is based on the fact that hypoglycemia is normally a potent stimulant of GH secretion. Patients are given an insulin infusion until their serum glucose drops below 40. In normal patients, a surge in GH will result. If the peak GH following the insulin challenge is less than expected (ie, <5.1), the test is considered positive for GHD. The test is contraindicated in patients with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease or with seizure disorder and in patients older than 65 years.

The GHRH-arginine test is the more commonly used test. It does not depend on lowering serum glucose and has fewer contraindications, but is relatively contraindicated in severe liver and kidney disease. The GHRH-arginine test may be less accurate in patients with acute GHD of a hypothalamic origin (ie, recent irradiation).
Various other tests have been proposed, but none are as accurate as these two.
The presence of deficiencies in 3 or more pituitary axes strongly suggests the presence of GHD, and in this context provocative testing is optional.

Consider evaluation for GHD via provocative testing in adults who have a history of hypothalamic/pituitary disease, or intracranial surgery or irradiation and in children who are more than 2 SDs below average height for age.
Retest children treated for GHD as adults unless they have a known irreversible cause of GHD.

When children with known irreversible causes of GHD achieve adulthood (generally 18 years of age), stop GH replacement and measure the IGF-I level 1 month later. If it remains low, they are considered to have persistent GHD, and there is no need for further provocative testing.
Low IGF-I levels strongly suggest but do not diagnose impaired GH secretion; normal IGF-I levels do not rule out the disease.

The experience from worldwide studies of GHD in children shows that the earlier treatment begins, the greater the gains in stature that can be expected. If treatment is delayed until near or at the time of puberty, children will gain little in stature and will remain below their theoretical height potential.
GH replacement with recombinant GH is the standard of care; start with low doses and titrate every 1 to 2 months based on clinical, biochemical, and/or adverse responses. B

GH treatment is most likely to benefit those patients who have more severe clinical and biochemical abnormalities and should be encouraged in such patients. Weekly pegylated recombinant human growth hormone is an effective option.B

GH replacement with recombinant GH is the standard of care. Diagnosis and initial therapy should be confirmed by an endocrinologist. Interpretation of provocative testing can be complex and confusing to those not familiar with the tests. Initial dose adjustments are based on biochemical markers and clinical symptoms and thus should be managed by someone very familiar with both aspects of the disease. Primary care follow-up is appropriate for patients doing well on a stable dose of GH.

Typical starting doses for adults are 1 to 2 IU/m2/d, although the doses may be given only 3 times a week (ie, 4 IU/m2 given 3 times a week is 1.7 IU/m2/d). Titrate the doses every 1 to 2 months based on clinical, biochemical (IGF-I levels), and/or adverse responses. Based on the final dosing of these responses and not solely on body surface area or weight. Once the patient is stable, monitor once or twice a year.

A systematic review identified 8 RCTs and cohort studies with 2549 children comparing once weekly pegylated recombinant human growth hormone (PEGrhGH, also called lonapegsomatropin) with daily rhGH. Weekly PEGrhGH was at least as effective as daily rhGH, and the 0.2 mg/kg/week dose was more effective at achieving height increase than 0.1 mg/kg/week with similar tolerability.
GH treatment is contraindicated in the presence of an active malignancy.
Surgical therapy is only indicated if the cause of the GHD is an untreated pituitary or hypothalamic neoplasm.
There are no dietary restrictions for adults or children with GHD.
Diagnosis and initial therapy should be confirmed by an endocrinologist. Interpretation of provocative testing can be complex and confusing to those not familiar with the tests.
The initial dose adjustments are based on biochemical markers and clinical symptoms and thus should be managed by someone very familiar with both aspects of the disease.
Children diagnosed and treated at an early age with appropriate dosing of recombinant GH can achieve adult stature in the normal adult range. B

Adults treated for GHD demonstrate improvement in body composition, exercise capacity, and quality of life measures; those with more severe disease (based on clinical and biochemical markers) are more likely to benefit. B
Untreated GHD increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. Unfortunately, there is limited evidence that GH replacement decreases these risks. C

There is some evidence that normal GH levels decline with age, so provocative testing may not be as accurate in patients older than 65 years, unless the cutoff for a positive test is adjusted. There is no consensus on what the correct cutoffs are in the older population.

GHD is rarely discovered in pregnancy, as GHD severe enough to be treated generally impairs fertility. Patients well controlled on a stable dose of GH replacement may continue the same dose throughout pregnancy.
